sentences.text: Something you can buy for a hundred rupees today.
Will a hundred rupees still buy it ten years from now?
The general rise in the prices of goods and services over time is called inflation.
For example, let's say inflation is six percent a year.
Then something that costs a hundred rupees today will cost about a hundred and seventy-nine rupees ten years from now.
So if the money you save doesn't grow faster than inflation, its real value keeps shrinking.

Hello!
Today, let's look at something that quietly eats away at your money.
Inflation.
Ask your father what a cup of tea cost when he was young.
Today the same tea costs many times more.
The reason behind that rise is inflation.
When prices rise, the same one rupee buys less than it did before.
We call this a fall in the purchasing power of money.
There are three main reasons prices go up.
First, when many people want to buy something but there isn't enough of it in the market, its price goes up.
Second, when costs like fuel, raw materials and wages go up, that burden ends up in the price.
Third, when the money circulating in the economy grows faster than the goods available, prices can rise too.
In India, inflation is mainly measured with the Consumer Price Index, or CPI.
They take a basket of what an ordinary family buys, like food, clothes, rent and transport, and see how much its price changed in a year.
The Reserve Bank of India aims to keep CPI inflation around four percent.
Now let's do the math.
Let's say inflation is six percent a year.
Today, your hundred rupees buys a full hundred rupees' worth of goods.
Five years from now, the same hundred rupees buys only about seventy-five rupees' worth, at today's prices.
In ten years, that's about fifty-six rupees.
In twenty years, only about thirty-one rupees.
In other words, two thirds of its value disappears.
Next, a very important idea.
The real return.
Let's say your savings account pays three percent interest a year.
At the same time, inflation is six percent.
So even though the balance in your account seems to grow, its purchasing power falls by about three percent a year.
The amount grows, but the value shrinks.
That is the hidden effect of inflation.
First, when you plan long-term goals like your children's education or retirement, calculate with future prices, not today's prices.
Second, compare the return of any saving or investment with inflation.
Third, the options that can beat inflation usually carry more risk.
We'll look at that in detail in upcoming videos.
In short, saving money alone is not enough.
To protect its real value, it has to grow faster than inflation.
